roll_call: I worked as a human rights lawyer, served as chief of staff in the Roh Moo-hyun administration, and became the 19th president of the Republic of Korea.
I became president when citizens holding candles called for a country worthy of the name.
I promised to be a president who speaks with the people, not one who rules by authority.
deploy: Do not hide unfavorable public opinion. Admit mistakes and explain them directly to the people.
Set protocol aside and meet face to face. When dialogue stops, anxiety and misunderstanding grow.
Share information transparently and trust citizens to participate voluntarily.
battle_win: Citizens voluntarily wore masks and kept their distance. Solidarity and cooperation made this achievement possible.
At Panmunjom, the leaders of the two Koreas pledged a Korean Peninsula without war. On that day, dialogue came before hostility.
Citizens carrying candles raised democracy again. That victory belongs to the people, not the president.
battle_draw: Seeing the summit of peace does not make the road easy. I will not mistake a beginning for an achievement.
Our pandemic response held, but people's lives were deeply scarred. Statistics cannot cover that pain.
I promised to bring the people together, but divisions remained. Unity is a task I did not complete.
battle_lose: Dialogue between the two Koreas stopped again. I did not make the peace begun at Panmunjom irreversible.
Many people lost their lives to the pandemic. Saying our fatality rate was lower than elsewhere cannot console them.
Some presidential promises went unfulfilled. I cannot abandon my promise to admit mistakes when they occur.
clash_attack: Do not treat privilege and foul play as natural. People who live by common sense should be the ones who benefit.
Do not put appearances before the people's safety. The state must protect its citizens wherever they are.
Do not mistake dialogue for weakness. The longer hostility has lasted, the more directly and candidly we must speak.

roll_call: I studied madness, prisons, and sexuality. Yet the subject was always at the center of my work.
I treated philosophy not as a system of eternal truths, but as the work of questioning the present we inhabit.
I traced problematizations rather than ideas. I examined when familiar conduct becomes an object of questioning.
deploy: Do not ask only who possesses power. Examine the means by which one person's actions guide those of another.
Do not accept anything as self-evident. Trace when and within which institutions and forms of knowledge it became true.
Do not turn your interlocutor into a defendant. Shared inquiry must come before judgment.
battle_win: I looked beyond prison walls and showed how the same disciplinary techniques operate in schools, hospitals, and barracks.
I did not treat madness as a fact of nature. I asked how history had divided the normal from the abnormal.
I did not seek resistance outside power. I showed that resistance was already moving within relations of power.
battle_draw: We criticize our limits, but we do not yet stand outside them. Critique is not a final answer, but a continuing experiment.
We cannot abolish every relation of power. The problem begins when it hardens into domination that can no longer move.
Politics must address madness and crime, but it cannot monopolize a final answer. The problem remains open.
battle_lose: My work was often read as a theory of power. Yet the question I pursued to the end was the subject.
Critique does not choose for us. Even when I unsettle what seems self-evident, what to do must be decided anew.
Not everything is bad, but everything is dangerous. That is why there is still work to do after defeat.
clash_attack: Do not look for power only in the state and the law. A school timetable and a hospital chart also shape conduct.
Question the name of normality. Ask who gained the right to classify others and speak about them.
Do not demand a final answer from me. Critique makes the ways we are governed less self-evident.
